title: Noble Truth
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach's talk emphasizes the importance of redefining nobility beyond traditional notions of wealth or status, instead highlighting inner qualities like wisdom, poise, and kindness as the true markers of a noble life. They suggest that this understanding can be applied to our daily experiences, particularly when faced with challenging circumstances, by embracing our own "ordinary mind" - the present moment and our personal experience - rather than seeking external validation or solutions. By letting go of reactions and expectations, we can cultivate trust in ourselves and life, leading to balance, openness, and stability.

I'll take the mask off so you can see or hear, or feel or taste, if you can actually really hear me.
Oh, thank you.
Thank you very much.

And on the surpassed, penetrating and perfect Dharma, is rarely a hundred thousand million kalpas, having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.
So good morning, everyone here in person for sesshin.
And good morning to everyone out in the Zoom zendo.
Welcome.
Glad that you can all join.
And thank you once again for the invitation to be here with you for this practice period.
I'm really delighted to be able to share this time with you.
And I have an opportunity to speak about something that has been in my heart and in my mind for a very long time.
So this is the first time I've tried to really articulate it in this way.
And I'm glad to do it among friends.
So tomorrow ends the formal study for our practice period and the teachings that we've had of Thich Nhat Hanh and our Shuso.
I wonder what questions have come up for you this practice period.
What will you carry on after the practice period ends?
What's in your heart and what's in your mind?
I want to talk today about the whole idea of noble, the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Noble Path.
What does that mean to you?
And how have I come to understand it after a very long time?
And it turns out to be not at all what I thought it would be.
So Buddha's first teachings are the noble teachings.

And they're usually thought of being noble because they're seen as a way to live a wholesome life, an awakened and enlightened way of being, and noble because it can liberate us from the suffering and the self-inflicted burden that we carry, that quiver of second arrows to set them aside that drain our life and our energy.
Nobility is usually associated with activity that is honest, generous, and courageous.
But it is quite possible.
It's my observed experience, and it may be yours too, that activities that on the surface can seem like this actually have a tinge of something else,
something that looks to be generous or charitable, can have some quality of being condescending or wanting a favor in return.
Something that may appear to be courageous may have a tint of being power-hungry or angry or vengeful underneath.
So sometimes what looks to be like generous, kind, or courageous can have something else underneath that looks like good, but what's not penetrated through deep down inside.
I'd never really stopped to think about the word noble and the Four Noble Truths or how what that lofty word means in terms of what a practitioner aspires to in a lived life.
You know, it just seems like it's too big and too grand a word.
But only about a decade or so ago I remembered a story of something that had happened to me when I was young, maybe nine or ten years old, and it planted a seed.
Maybe most of us who are here have something that happened that was a little touchstone for us early in our life that we look back on.
And this was kind of surprisingly for me one of those stories that, as I say, was subconscious for a long time.
It's probably Easter.
We didn't go to church very often.
And my father never went.
It was always my mother and I, even though it was the church of his growing up and not hers.
We were walking along the street leaving the church at the end of the day.
It was in the sixties and it was in that time that it was still being Catholic was still a little bit strange or other.
I remember my parents talking just a few years earlier about whether John F.
Kennedy could be elected as president because he was a Catholic or not.
This was a very Protestant, Northern European kind of suburb.
But we were walking along and it happened to be on the same street as the Catholic Church.
I didn't even know we had one.
And we saw two nuns walking towards us in their habits and their cornets, you know, the full regala.
And they looked so calm and peaceful, alive, you know, not stern at all.
But there was something very collected and gathered and unusual about them.
Their dress was simple and well ordered, you know, not a lot of busts and hoopla.
It looks like things were in their place without a lot of to do.
My mother was my mother had a kind of reserve that belayed a deep sense of humanity that she had.
Her elder brother had fought in World War II at Normandy on D-Day and had returned a man quite softened like a very tender leather by his experiences of having survived that event.
And as we walked along the street, my mother said to me, as we pass these nuns, very simple passing of two ordinary people on the street, kind of.
And she said to me, that's a noble life.
I don't know quite why that stayed with me.
I don't know at nine or ten what I thought noble meant.
Usually noble means someone in a castle somewhere or maybe the Queen of England, an aristocrat who has everything that they need and lives a life that's relatively easy.
One of the deficits, perhaps above the vicissitudes of life.
I didn't make that connection with this experience and I didn't really think much more about it than that.
But it's left me with a question.
Noble men or women are usually wise and poised, dignified, as I say, above the usual vicissitudes of what it means that most of us have to struggle with.
Buddha, however, was born in a noble caste, but he was a radical, right?
His teachings and his ideas were that everyone had the possibility of living a life that was above the vicissitudes in a certain way of the normal struggles of living.
Everyone.
I know it took him a little while to catch on to the fact that women could be part of his sangha too, but that came with time and the right circumstances.
He came to understand as long as people have medicine, food and shelter, everyone could find spiritual and emotional well-being in this life.

And he prescribed the practices that we've studied this practice period, practices that I think of as attitude or as Noam and Tim said yesterday, orientation, the right view, the right understanding or intention as a foundation.

Really the heart of the practice of the eightfold noble path or mindfulness, paying very close and complete attention to one's inside and outside experience, concentration and the right kind of applying oneself wholeheartedly and effort.
And to do that in every aspect of life, speech, livelihood and in action.
So that together can lead to a noble life.
Well, in Theravada tradition, I practiced at that tradition in my early years as a Buddhist practitioner.
I think the basic understanding is that there's a natural brightness of mind that exists and by applied purification of observation, it's possible to reveal that brightness.
Maybe not in this lifetime, but in many lifetimes, one can become virtuous, honest, upright, worthy, unselfish, generous, magnanimous and especially kind and caring for people.
Not from an outwardly directed practice so much, but from this deep, concentrated, mindful sitting, radical mindfulness and a deep commitment to wake up to one's liberation.
But I had a question about all that.
That takes a very long time.

And part of that question came for me because in my work, for those of you who don't know, I've been a physician for a long time and I work particularly with people in the midst of really serious, difficult illness in the last usually year years of their lives.
And I kept finding that so many of the people that I took care of evoke this feeling of nobility in me.
That's really how the story came back to me.
And I was trying to puzzle that together, because on the surface of it, their lives didn't look very noble.
One of them turned out to be a Buddhist practitioner but none of them were people who do what we do in order to wake up.

A Korean restaurant owner who coming to this country, arriving in Alaska and finding that she was in an unfaithful, untenable marriage became a ruthless businesswoman, ruthless, in order to provide for the daughter that she hardly helped raise.
She was so busy.

An Academy Award-winning software engineer in his early thirties who drove everyone crazy by his exactitude about what he expected in his care and as he tried to fight his cancer and live with the complications of his chemotherapy.

A man who came from a very damaged childhood who had a foray into drug dealing and things that he later said I don't feel very proud about, who wound up being a social worker for the homeless while staying homeless himself.
He didn't feel like he deserved anything else.
All of them had incredibly had a nobility about them.
It's really hard to pin by the usual definitions, I think.
I've wondered about that.
They all found their way to manifest some quality that I would call noble.
The end of life can do that.
In a certain way, it's almost an easy foray, even though it's kind of a shame to wait that long.
And it's kind of surprising to think that this has some echoes of the three seals or marks that we've been studying, I think.

Really recognizing our sense of impermanence when you get that there really is no way out except straight ahead, which sometimes takes us to the last months or days of life to turn towards to see that we're really going to die.
We become like a milkweed that opens and disperses the seeds of that which we have done in our lives.
Or as one reviews their connections in life, what their life has been, who they've been with, what they've done.
There's this deep sense of gratitude and kind of recognition of how the pieces of one's life all fit together that give people an ease.
That was a big clue for me.
And it may not be so overt.
I don't think many of these people, if any of them, would have articulated that or actually had those conversations.
But I could see it.
The work I do is very intimate.
I hear people's stories and I really have a sense of who they are as people.
So there's a radical acceptance that can come.
And there was something about what I was seeing in those people that was subtly that, I think.
I think our path in Zen is somewhat different than the basic way in which the Buddha laid out the Eightfold Noble Path and the way it's often practiced in Theravadan tradition.
So here's another story about kind of coming to see that.
When I found Zen practice and recognized that I was home, I threw myself in a thousand percent.
I was so happy and so committed, so joyous.
Anything there was to do, crawling under the ton to dust over the heat vents, whatever it was, I would do it in spades with quite a bit of just happiness.
Maybe you've all had that kind of feeling.
I know some of you know exactly what that is.
And I didn't think I was thinking much about me.
And then one day for the morning Jundo, we sit facing the wall at Berkeley.
And I go every morning at 5:40.
And my teacher, Sojun Mel Weitsman, was there every morning.
He would do the Jundo, and we would go by, putting my hands in Gassho like we do.
One morning, I caught myself not just listening for the footsteps to know when to do it, but watching to see whether he noticed my Gassho and how lovely it was.
Did you ever catch yourself doing something like that?
It looks like good, right?
There we are.
It looks like I was doing good.
I hadn't really realized this.
We are doing the Shuso ceremony tomorrow, and we have the script.
Nomon Tim sent me the script last week.
I looked at the last page and thought, "Ordinary mind is the way."
That was Kate McKenna's Koan.
Why is that here?
Then I realized yesterday, thanks to Benji Bob, that that's what we use all the time every day.
I'm going to use it too.
Case 19 of the Mumonkan: Joshua asked Nansen, "What is the way?"
And Nansen answers, "Ordinary mind is the way."
Boy, is that a steep mountain.
Ordinary, capital O, not the diluted ordinary mind, but not the diluted ordinary mind, right?

Ordinary, capital, like capital L in life, which Yama Roshi says—life, living life, the universal life, or the self becoming the self, or the self doing the self, small self, large self, the large sense, the integrated sense, the ever connected sense.
Ordinary mind in that way.
Ordinary mind is our own personal mind, liberated.
Joshua continues to ask, "How about finding this way?
How do I go about doing that?"
Don't we all want to know?
Go talk to the teacher and say, "I got this problem.
Why am I still stuck on it?
How do I figure this out?"
But it's not like that.
It isn't something that you can look for.
It's actually right here.
Do you know that?
It's actually right here.
You have everything right here.

Ordinary mind uses this life right now, at this moment, the life that we might normally think of as the problem—the problem, the divorce, the job that's not working out, the flood that hit your house, the illness that your partner has—everything that is not working out is this ordinary mind, too.
It is this life with which you live it and manifest Buddha's way.
There's nothing out of place.
My teacher, Sojun Mel Weitsman, who was Norman Fischer's teacher and Norman Tim's grandfather of the Dharma, used to be described as ordinary.
Any event at San Francisco Zen Center, they'd always hold up his ordinary mind.
Sojun said, "I never wanted anything for myself."
Imagine that.
If a student came to him, he helped.
If a student left, he wasn't worried about it.
He wasn't worried about himself or his teaching.
He cared about the student, but he didn't cling.
He trusted the student's own path and way, but he was always available.
His life was just an offering.
This case is about wanting and realizing the practice by coming face to face with ourselves and accepting that we have what we need right here and now.
It takes a lot of effort.
In his commentary on this koan, Shibayama likens accepting the spiritual work and the effort that it takes to like receiving a jet iron black ball that's flying towards you.
Can you imagine what that's like to take that on?
For me, it's like it hits me in the stomach, knocks the wind out of me, the effort that it takes.
And then you just swallow it whole, chew it up.
You can't spit out any of it.
All of our life, we take into this moment.
It's like Zorba the Greek says, you take the whole catastrophe and live it.
Another Zen practitioner, another Zen story, comes from case 38 of the Book of Serenity, Rinzai or Linji's koan, "True man of no rank."
This actually got handed to me as a statement during my Shuso ceremony, which had a lot of people and a lot of senior people.
I was struggling to hold on, and at one point our vice abbot said, "I think I'm meeting a true man of no rank.
I just had to give up."
Master Rinzai was strong and iconoclastic.

He was known for his dramatic actions, hitting or shouting, anything that he could do to wake people out and kind of jar them out of their usual conceptual teaching, kind of fierce and a little fearsome to our contemporary way of thinking of things.
In this koan, he famously gets up on the teaching seat and he says, "Show me a true person of no rank."
No one steps forward, no one does or says anything.
And then he says, "There she is, there he is, going in and out through the holes of your head."
You've had that experience.

Maybe it was the first time that you were in a new place, in nature, or in a foreign country, somehow communicating with people in a language that you've never spoken, but there's an immediacy of connection that allows you to do that, the freshness of the air that you've never experienced before.
It's just ordinary air by a stream.
It's completely new.
What is that?

The sense doors are open, just receiving and experience everything before we have any opinion, any idea about a place, we must experience it as something that we don't—it's not something that we like or dislike, want or not.
A true person of no rank doesn't put their ideas in the way of their experience.
Sojun used to say, "I don't get caught by anything, that's my secret.
I don't get caught by anything."
That means not getting caught by his own ideas or opinions.
He wasn't perfect at that, but he was pretty good.
And not being caught by other people's reactions or emotions.

That means for us, as we've been talking about and studying our minds this practice period, that we come to know our own pressure points, the places where we go in reaction under certain times of duress, our kind of habit energy that leads us to be more irritable, more judging, more shut down, more tired.
And we open to those and allow ourselves to receive from a deeper in place.
When we can do that, we can often connect with the situation in another way.

We can have a little distance from our emotion and our reactivities, whatever our habit is, and allow it just to be what it is, maybe with a light hearted giggle, "There I am again," or just with an ease where the energy of that reaction doesn't go anywhere.
It just drops.
Remember my first real experience of seeing that was with Blanche Hartman, who was the first woman abbot at San Francisco Zen Center.
I was with her in the sewing room, sewing my priest Okesa.
And Blanche had a very precise, she was a scientist by training, she had a very precise kind of persnickety mind in a certain way, she could be really tight.
But she would catch herself and just give a light hearted smile, and it would just all drop and open, and we just had to love her for it.
It's like that.
Just watching the time here, 10:30 is the end point, something like that, 11:30.

So there's a quality of balance, openness, stability, and confidence that comes by not getting pulled around by emotions, reactions, ideas, and a real growing trust in life, growing trust really in the Dharma.
There's a wonderful story about Suzuki Roshi in this regard.
He was in Japan during World War II and was running the small family temple.
Not a lot of practitioners, really very poor, hard time, people didn't have enough to eat.
Most of the priests were going out and getting other jobs to try and support himself because the Donka, the lay community, didn't have money or resources to support the temple.
And he said, "If my practice is good enough, I'll be supported."
He decided there was a piece of dirt in front of the temple that he would make a garden and grow food there because his family was hungry, and so were other people.
He removed the rocks, tilled the soil, planted a garden.
He did it with great care, and so the crop was really pretty good, and he had plenty of food, more than what they needed.
So he gave it away to people, and people were so grateful that they brought him rice.
The rice, so many people brought him rice out of gratitude for what he was doing, that there was more rice than what the temple could use, so he gave that away, too.
So there was plenty for everyone to go around out of his efforts.
Suzuki Roshi said, "We are firmly protected from inside.
That is our spirit.
We are firmly protected from inside.
That is our spirit."
It's the spirit behind right effort.
We are protected from inside always, incessantly, so we don't expect any help from the outside.
We don't accept it.
We don't expect it.
But somehow we're turning the wheel of the Dharma, and we're riding the wheel of the Dharma.
This is from one of the talks in "Not Always So Called Supported From Within."

So when we accept things as they are, not just the who of our lives, but accept everything—our habitual patterns, our personality, our body with its limitations, the path in life that's been cast, "Oh, why did I wind up doing this instead of that?"—and all the external circumstances.
It's like being willing to play with the cards life has dealt you.
We all have a set of cards.
And I feel like, at least for me, I've spent a lot of my life wishing I had had different cards, or I could put these down and pick up some other ones.
But I've come to really understand and appreciate this is what I got.
And this is how it's playing out.
And I'm just going to throw myself in.
It's a deep-seated trust in one's life.

It's so much easier knowing that we live in Indra's network of interdependent origination, that we're one part of the spinning Dharma wheel for this vast net where every being is one of the jewels, where the fibers cross, and any place you pick, the whole thing vibrates in activity.
And each of our life is an integral part of the functioning of that net.
So use it.
Use what you've been given.
That's part of the ask here.
So when a person has a terminal illness, the best response, the fortunate response, the courageous and real response, is to trust all of what life has been.
And I would say we all have that situation in our life sooner or later.
And that, perhaps, is what is noble, honest, kind, courageous, and generous.
Thank you very much for your attention.
For once, I didn't run to the bitter end.
We should equally spend to every being and place, with the truth there is way.
Thank you.
